taxonomyNote: Until 1997 Alabama populations were called northern zigzag salamander (P. dorsalis); NatureServe notes Highton (1997) recognized P. ventralis as distinct from P. dorsalis and P. angusticlavius.
fieldMarks: Small, 2.5-3.5 in; sides brown to dark gray with a yellowish or orange stripe down the back that may be straight, wavy or lobed.
Brownish-gray unstriped morph occurs; small white flecks on back and sides give a metallic look.
Belly gray or black, mottled or speckled with orange or red; most Alabama specimens have 18 costal grooves.
behavior: Forages on the forest floor for small invertebrates.
Completely terrestrial with no aquatic larval stage; nests presumably in subterranean cavities in summer.
Found under rocks, logs or leaves by day.
habitat: Upland rocky hardwood woodlands, ravines, seepages, rubble and cave mouths; often under rotten logs and rocks.
range: Illinois and Indiana south to north and central Alabama, mainly in the Southwestern Appalachians and Interior Plateau uplands. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Webster's salamander
lookalikes.howToTell: Basically identical in appearance; separated by geographic range and genetics, and in P. websteri the stripe tends to be wavy only on the front half of the body.
